expected_value.method:
The expected saving from the Burnham plan: a calibrated distribution of paths and a stratified sample of full runs.

Why an expected value
---------------------
The triple lock takes a maximum each year, and the Burnham plan pays at least
max(CPI, 2.5%) but otherwise only what keeps the pension on its 2029-30 earnings
path. The saving comes from years when the higher of CPI and 2.5% runs ahead of
earnings: the triple lock keeps that gain for good, while the Burnham plan's
level waits for earnings to catch up. A single central path, on which earnings
lead from 2031, gives almost none. The expected saving is a weighted mean of
the saving over paths, each saving a full model run.

1. Draws
--------
``N_DRAWS`` paths of the monthly model (ts_monthly: a VAR on monthly log
changes of the CPI index and AWE, residual-bootstrap shocks), August 2026 to
December 2039. Every annual measure, the statutory inputs (September CPI,
May-July AWE) and the calendar-year ones, comes from the same simulated months.

2. Calibration
--------------
* Means: the smoothest monthly drift path that makes the draws' mean calendar
  CPI and earnings growth equal the central path in every year 2027-2039
  (``ts_monthly.shift_to_calendar_means``). Every draw moves by the same
  amount, so the shocks and their dependence are the model's own. (Entropy
  tilting to the same means, the earlier approach, keeps about 1,000 of 50,000
  draws' worth of weight: the model's own means sit far from the OBR's.)
* Dynamics: entropy tilting (minimal change in weights) so that, jointly with
  the means, the expected per-path variance of the statutory real-wage gap
  (May-July AWE minus September CPI, 2026-2038) and the expected rate at which
  the lead passes between the two inputs match history.
* Not targeted: the share of years in which both inputs are below 2.5%. The
  OBR's central forecast itself has earnings below 2.5% from 2027 to 2030, so
  matching history's lower share would fight the means. It is reported.

The history window and the treatment of 2020-21 (furlough-era earnings) set
the dynamics targets; every combination is solved and reported. The primary
is chosen on the expected-value backtest (``ev_backtest``) and the past-years
check: the drift shift alone (the OBR's means, the model's own dynamics). In
the backtest, tilting to the dynamics of the history before each origin made
the expected gap more biased, not less, and the past-years check puts the
realised 2012-start gap at the 56th percentile of the untilted model fitted
before 2011 but the 93rd of the tilted one. The dynamics tilts are
sensitivities, computed from the same full runs by reweighting.

3. Full runs
------------
The draws with identical rates under both rules in every year have a saving of
exactly zero (both runs get the same inputs); they form their own stratum and
one of them is run to confirm it. The rest are split into ``N_STRATA`` strata
of equal probability on the 2039-40 gap in the full new State Pension (rule
arithmetic on the weekly rate), paths are allocated across strata in
proportion to probability x the gap's spread in the stratum (Neyman), with at
least ``MIN_PER_STRATUM``, and drawn within each stratum with probability
proportional to weight (with replacement). Each is a full model run of both
rules (engine.run_path). The estimate for any output is sum_h W_h x its mean
over stratum h's runs. Its Monte Carlo variance adds path sampling
sum_h W_h^2 s_h^2 / n_h and first phase
sum_h W_h [s_h^2 + (m_h-m)^2] / N_DRAWS, including the zero stratum.
For reweighted calibrations, the first phase instead uses target-distribution
moments and the effective number of macro draws, (sum w)^2 / sum w^2.
Both components are reported separately and do not measure model uncertainty.
Microcosm runs a paired subsample (the first
paths drawn in each stratum), so the dataset difference is estimated from
paired runs.

dwp_uprating_analysis.definition: In any given year it will go up by at least inflation or 2.5% – and anything more that is needed to retain that value [the 2029-30 ratio to earnings]
dwp_uprating_analysis.model: Pensim3, DWP's dynamic microsimulation model (population and pension outcomes projected to 2100, ONS 2024-based population projections)
dwp_uprating_analysis.coverage: Great Britain; direct Annually Managed Expenditure, no tax or debt interest effects; rounded to the nearest £1bn; one deterministic uprating path, not stated

method_limitations: Each rise follows the triple lock's convention of September CPI and May-July earnings (the statute requires at least earnings). The central path uses the OBR's September-quarter CPI and April-June earnings for the Aprils 2028-2031 and its calendar-year long-term path after; the monthly model builds both measures from the same simulated months.
After 2030 the central path is the OBR's long-term projection, which it describes as not a forecast.

The expected value rests on one statistical model of CPI and earnings (a monthly VAR fitted to 2000-2026), shifted so its calendar-year averages equal the OBR's. Its statutory inputs are off the OBR's quarterly figures in 2026-2028 (before the switch), and its September 2026 CPI is simulated from August's rather than fixed. Its backtest rests on twelve overlapping four-year windows.
In every run April 2027's benefit uprating is the model's own calendar-2026 CPI forecast (2.3%), not September 2026 CPI, which is published on 21 October 2026.

The population is aged statically, not dynamically: each survey record stands for a person of its age in every year. After the data's calibration year (2025-26) household weights follow the ONS 2024-based projection's growth by age and sex; records top-coded at 80 get represented ages from 80 to 105; and each year's State Pension type follows the person's birth cohort. Later retirees' pension amounts come from today's records of the same age, and deaths, migration and contribution histories are not simulated. Pensioners living abroad are outside the survey.

In the calibration year the weights are the data's own, but policyengine-uk uprates them from the survey year by less than the data build materialized them, so they sit 0.44% below the calibrated levels (policyengine-uk-data#538), and every later year carries that.
Rents and council tax stay at their 2030 amounts after 2030, and dividend, property, savings and self-employment income do not follow the path.

In the survey runs Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them: nobody the plan makes newly entitled starts claiming, which understates those offsets and so overstates the net saving.

Concentration diagnostics remain private until support checks show at least ten contributing records in each reported total and each recoverable complement. Selecting ten records alone does not establish that ten records have nonzero contributions.

Every rule follows the triple lock to April 2029. The Burnham plan from April 2030 rises by at least the higher of CPI and 2.5% and by whatever else keeps the pension at its 2029-30 ratio to earnings, as DWP defines it; its top-up to the earnings path is rounded up to 0.1 point.

Only the basic and new State Pension change between the rules. Under both, the additional State Pension rises with September CPI and the Pension Credit guarantee with May-July earnings (the statutory minimum), and the State Pension age follows the law's timetable by date of birth, so every age of 67 and over is above it from 2028-29. There is no behavioural response.
Reported State Pension below State Pension age is not counted, as none is payable before it; every run records how many survey records report one (state_pension_accounting).

policyengine-uk pays Scotland's Pension Age Winter Heating Payment at £100 a household without a qualifying benefit from winter 2025, where the regulations pay £203.40 (£305.10 at 80) a person living alone (policyengine-uk#2138), and it has no 25p age addition at 80 (policyengine-uk#2139).

The primary model/data pair is the policyengine 6.2.6 certified UK bundle: policyengine-uk 2.125.1, policyengine-core 3.33.0 and Enhanced FRS from policyengine-uk-data 1.58.0. Microcosm is an uncertified sensitivity.
Costs are in cash terms (nominal £) for the UK; DWP's figures are for Great Britain. Each path run in the results file also gives its saving for Great Britain.

assumptions.title: Today's pensioners, reweighted to the ONS projection
assumptions.text: Survey ages do not move between years to 2039-40, though some differ from their survey values. Each person's State Pension type follows their cohort: basic if they reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016, new otherwise. Household weights are raked each year to the ONS population projection by age and sex, so the number of pensioners follows it. DWP's costing projects the population; ours reweights the survey rather than ageing it.

assumptions.title: Model-conditional paths
assumptions.text: Model-conditional expected value; original monthly VAR(1) bootstrap passes the frozen C2 statutory screen. Its paths are shifted to the OBR's average forecast. Reweighting the same full runs to match how much the gap between earnings growth and CPI varied in the past and how often the lead switched (in some versions also how often the 2.5% floor binds) gives separate point estimates, the lowest £5.6bn gross (standard error £1.0bn) and the highest £12.4bn, which rests on about 141 effective runs (standard error £0.5bn). This range does not include another model of prices and earnings: Student-t and Gaussian versions are tested against past forecasts (Methodology tab) but not run through the full fiscal model. The scenario envelope is reported separately; it is not a probability interval.

assumptions.title: Survey benefit baselines above DWP's
assumptions.text: In 2026-27 the survey has 1.48m Pension Credit claims in Great Britain against DWP's 1.31m, and £7.5bn of pension-age Housing Benefit against £7.3bn. On the same 40 paths, the Microcosm dataset gives a net saving £0.5bn higher (standard error £0.0bn).

benchmarks.title: State Pension uprating analysis 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: "-£15 billion" in "2039 to 2040" (Table 1: "In-year AME savings (nominal terms, rounded to nearest billion, negative values denote savings)"); "-£11 billion" in "real terms, 2025 to 2026 prices" (Table 2)
benchmarks.comparison: Adjusted triple lock (the Burnham plan) vs the triple lock: State Pension spending in 2039-40, nominal, Great Britain; direct effects on AME only, no tax or debt interest
benchmarks.note: DWP applies one uprating path, which it does not publish, in Pensim3, its dynamic microsimulation model, for Great Britain, rounded to £1bn. Ours is the expected gross saving over calibrated paths, each a full run on the Enhanced FRS for the UK, with survey ages held fixed.

benchmarks.title: Long-term economic determinants, March 2026 EFO
benchmarks.figure_text: "Average earnings growth plus 0.6 percentage points" (the note on the 'Triple lock' growth rate, sheet "Growth rate assumptions", column "Notes on 2025 Long-term economic determinants")
benchmarks.comparison: The OBR's long-term growth-rate assumption for triple-lock uprating, above average earnings growth (points a year)
benchmarks.note: The OBR's premium is an assumption for its long-term projections; in the sheet's 2026 column the 'Triple lock' rate is 0.56 points above average earnings growth (4.31% against 3.75% a year). Ours is the expected triple-lock rise less May-July earnings growth for the April 2034-2039 rises (inputs of 2033-2038) under the primary distribution: rule arithmetic, not a fiscal figure.

benchmarks.title: Fiscal risks and sustainability - July 2025
benchmarks.figure_text: "we estimate that uprating by the triple lock rather than earnings will have added £15.5 billion (0.5 per cent of GDP) to state pension spending annually by 2029-30. This is around three times higher than the £5.2 billion we estimate the triple lock would have cost by that point under initial assumptions"
benchmarks.comparison: Triple lock vs earnings uprating since its introduction in April 2012: extra State Pension spending in 2029-30; the £5.2bn is that cost on the assumptions of the original 2010 costing and its long-run expectation of rises 0.2 points a year above earnings
benchmarks.note: OBR compares the triple lock with earnings uprating since 2012, in 2029-30. Ours is the gross saving in 2026-27 had the Burnham plan, which keeps the higher of CPI and 2.5% as a floor, started in April 2012.

benchmarks.title: What a ratchet! (Curtice and Clegg)
benchmarks.figure_text: "The OBR estimates spending on the State Pension would have been £12.6 billion lower this year with earnings-linked uprating than it is set to be with triple lock uprating, which we estimate would be a net saving of around £9 billion when we take account of lower income tax receipts and higher means-tested benefit spending."
benchmarks.comparison: Triple lock vs earnings-linked uprating, State Pension spending "this year" (2026-27 when RF wrote): £12.6bn gross is the OBR's estimate, £9bn net of income tax and means-tested benefits is RF's
benchmarks.note: RF's summary describes the same £12.6bn as against "a smoothed earnings link since 2012"; the report's own text attributes it to the OBR, against earnings-linked uprating. Ours is the net saving in 2026-27 had the Burnham plan (which keeps a CPI and 2.5% floor) started in April 2012.

benchmarks.title: Fiscal risks and sustainability - July 2026
benchmarks.figure_text: State pension spending, "which is projected to rise from 5 per cent of GDP to around 9 per cent of GDP over the projection period in the baseline. This is driven by population ageing and the cost of triple-lock uprating (calculated based on historical inflation and earnings volatility). In a scenario where the state pension is instead uprated in line with average earnings, state pension spending reaches around 7 per cent of GDP."
benchmarks.comparison: Triple lock vs earnings uprating over the 50-year projection to 2075-76, with the triple lock's cost calibrated to historical inflation and earnings volatility, % of GDP
benchmarks.note: A 50-year horizon in % of GDP with ageing; ours is in £bn for 2039-40, with survey ages held fixed. Same direction: once CPI and earnings vary, the ratchet costs far more than on a central path (see central.run.saving_bn).
